case_prompt: A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with five days of redness in the right eye, three days of photophobia, ocular pain, and slight blurriness. He denied ocular trauma, recent illness, or cold sores. His ophthalmic history included uncomplicated bilateral small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) six months earlier. He had begun nighttime continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy two weeks prior for newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea and noted increased right-eye dryness on awakening. On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed inferonasal conjunctival injection with sectoral ciliary flush and limbitis. At the 4 o’clock position, small peripheral corneal infiltrates were visible without epithelial defect or corneal staining. Diffuse lamellar keratitis (grade I) was noted beneath the SMILE cap margin, corresponding to the area of limbitis. Examination of the left eye revealed mild superficial punctate keratopathy. Both eyes showed inspissated Meibomian glands and posterior marginal telangiectasias.

sentences.text: A 37-year-old Caucasian man presented with five days of redness in the right eye, three days of photophobia, ocular pain, and slight blurriness.
He denied ocular trauma, recent illness, or cold sores.
His ophthalmic history included uncomplicated bilateral small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) six months earlier.
He had begun nighttime continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy two weeks prior for newly diagnosed obstructive sleep apnea and noted increased right-eye dryness on awakening.
On examination, uncorrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye.
Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed inferonasal conjunctival injection with sectoral ciliary flush and limbitis.
At the 4 o’clock position, small peripheral corneal infiltrates were visible without epithelial defect or corneal staining.
Diffuse lamellar keratitis (grade I) was noted beneath the SMILE cap margin, corresponding to the area of limbitis.
Examination of the left eye revealed mild superficial punctate keratopathy.
Both eyes showed inspissated Meibomian glands and posterior marginal telangiectasias.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Herpetic keratitis was considered as an infective cause of peripheral corneal inflammation—“Differential diagnosis considerations were given to various other possibilities including herpetic keratitis, peripheral stromal keratitis, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis including Mooren’s ulcer.” 2. Peripheral stromal keratitis was considered among the causes of peripheral infiltrates—“Differential diagnosis considerations were given to various other possibilities including herpetic keratitis, peripheral stromal keratitis, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis including Mooren’s ulcer.” 3. Peripheral ulcerative keratitis, including Mooren’s ulcer, was considered given the peripheral limbal involvement—“Differential diagnosis considerations were given to various other possibilities including herpetic keratitis, peripheral stromal keratitis, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis including Mooren’s ulcer.” 4. Ocular rosacea and keratitis associated with systemic vascular diseases or rheumatoid arthritis were also considered due to blepharitis signs—“In the setting of the appropriate patient past medical history or other applicable findings differential diagnoses could also have included ocular rosacea and keratitis associated with systemic vascular diseases or rheumatoid arthritis.” 5. All of these alternatives were excluded in favor of marginal keratitis because “Given the presence of limbitis and the absence of corneal staining or defect overlying the infiltrate, a diagnosis of marginal keratitis was made.”

selection.screen_reason: Sectoral injection with limbitis and peripheral infiltrates without staining, plus meibomian disease and new CPAP dryness, give marginal keratitis.
selection.second_look_note: Red painful photophobic eye after SMILE with new CPAP-related dryness frames the problem; slit-lamp limbitis with unstained peripheral infiltrates decides.
